If you work directly on the server, you run the risk that some sort of network interruption may cause problems.The ability to remember the past is critical for many levels of human behavior, from day-to-day behaviors, such as remembering to take medications or recognizing previously encountered people, places, and things, to other fundamental cognitive abilities, such as the development and use of language. Memory is central to who we are and how we behave, with knowledge about the past informing decisions about how to act in the present. Broadly, the objective of the research in the Stanford Memory Laboratory is to understand how memory is organized and supported by the mind and brain. A particular emphasis is placed on understanding the interaction between cognitive control and long-term memory, as well as on delineating the nature of "cross-talk" between different forms of memory (e.g., interactions between declarative and nondeclarative processes). In the course of these efforts, we further aim to characterize the functional contributions of prefrontal and medial temporal regions to learning and remembering.In our research, we adopt a multi-modal imaging approach that combines the spatial resolution of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with the temporal resolution of magnetoencephalography (MEG) and, more recently, electroencephalography (EEG). FMRI characterizes the functional contributions of specific brain regions to memory, and anatomical MRI guides the solutions for MEG/EEG analysis of cortical temporal dynamics. This approach is complemented by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)--a technique permitting the momentary disruption of local cortical activity in healthy individuals--thus affording a test of the necessity of cortical computations for memory. Recent applications of this integrative approach have contributed to knowledge about the neural mechanisms supporting memory, including demonstrating the necessity of specific structures for learning [Kahn et al., 2005] and the temporal profile of neural responses during remembering [Gonsalves et al., 2005]. As summarized below, our goal is to understand memory both at the neural and psychological levels.Memory is intimately involved in most, if not all, levels of human cognition, from the ability to temporarily remember a phone number or where you placed your keys to the acquisition of language and the ability to reason. Behavioral and neural data indicate that memory is not a unitary faculty, but rather consists of multiple systems that support learning and remembering, each with its own processing characteristics and neurobiological substrates. This lecture course will provide an advanced survey of what is known about memory, placing an emphasis on understanding the cognitive and neural architectures of working memory, declarative memory, and nondeclarative memory.Declarative memory supports the conscious remembrance of past experience, including the ability to discriminate novel from familiar stimuli and to recollect details about a prior encounter with a stimulus.This seminar will consider current debates regarding the cognitive and neural architecture of declarative memory, specifically focusing on recent efforts to address these controversies through application of functional neuroimaging (primarily fMRI and EEG).Through readings of conceptual "seed" articles and group discussion of neuroimaging investigations, the aim is to provide a forum in which new empirical efforts to address these debates may emerge. There are no prerequisites for this course, though a working understanding of memory and neuroimaging methods will prove useful.Cognitive control refers to processes that enable flexible behavior by biasing contextually relevant perceptual, mnemonic, and response representations or processing pathways. Cognitive control is central to volitional action, allowing us to work with memory, represent task/goal states, and override competing, inappropriate responses. This seminar will consider formal models of cognitive control, with group discussion focusing on how the models account for behavioral, functional neuroimaging, neuropsychological, and neurophysiological evidence regarding the nature of cognitive control.There are many opportunities in the lab to participate in behavioral and brain imaging studies. Behavioral studies typically last between 30 minutes and 2 hours and involve using a computer to perform memory tasks. Participants are presented with stimuli and are asked to perform simple cognitive tasks (e.g., they may be asked to determine/learn a rule that governs classification of the stimuli, or they may be asked to maintain the stimuli in short-term memory). Brain imaging studies typically last between 1 and 3 hours. Participants lie on an MR table within the magnet while structural and functional images are collected.In so doing, these mechanisms are thought to guide stimulus processing and the on-line maintenance of internal representations through the sustained allocation of attention to relevant stimulus features and long-term representations.In addition to exploring the functional organization of PFC, our research advances the perspective that PFC-mediated mechanisms are not restricted to stimulus processing, working memory, and response selection functions. Rather, we emphasize how long-term memory formation and retrieval depend on the “control of memory.” To this end, we aim to identify and characterize the nature of the control processes that contribute to the encoding of memories and that guide the retrieval of existing memories. We emphasize that these processes are not “memory” mechanisms per se, but rather are fundamental forms of cognitive control that are engaged in the service of memory. Accordingly, we focus on the interplay between PFC-mediated control processes, long-term representations that are stored in posterior neocortical association areas, and binding and retrieval mechanisms subserved by the medial temporal lobes (MTL). Some of our efforts to understand mnemonic control include delineation of the PFC mechanisms supporting (a) controlled retrieval from semantic memory, (b) episodic memory formation, and (c) episodic retrieval with and without recollection.Retrieving meaning in a context-relevant manner is critical to cognition. Doing so allows us to flexibly access information about concepts and objects in order to comprehend inputs and generate responses. Although on a continuum, there are two general routes to retrieving relevant semantic knowledge--automatic and controlled retrieval. Over the past seven years, our research has explored the neural mechanisms that support controlled semantic retrieval and that accompany the transition from controlled to automatic access.Building on this potential anatomic segregation, we recently tested whether controlled retrieval and selection are distinct VLPFC processes or whether these models reduce to a common mechanism [Badre et al., 2005]. Using factor analytic techniques, we obtained evidence for a meta-factor that accounted for behavioral variance across tasks evoking semantic competition and for functional variance in left mid-VLPFC (inferior frontal gyrus pars triangularis), supporting a generalized control process that selects relevant knowledge from amongst competitors. By contrast, left anterior VLPFC (inferior frontal gyrus pars orbitalis) was sensitive to cue-target associative strength, but not competition, consistent with a control process that retrieves knowledge that does not automatically come to mind. These observations, together with other evidence that mid-VLPFC resolves competition within working memory [Badre & Wagner, in press] and during episodic recollection [Dobbins & Wagner, in press], motivate a two-process model of VLPFC function during semantic access, with distinct mechanisms mediating controlled retrieval and post-retrieval selection [for discussion, see Badre et al., 2005].Central to understanding memory is determining why some experiences can be later remembered, whereas others are forgotten. One factor that may influence memory is the nature and extent of the cognitive control operations engaged during episodic encoding—that is, the process of transforming an experience into a durable memory trace such that it can be subsequently remembered. We have been testing the hypothesis that PFC control mechanisms guide episodic encoding by bringing task-relevant representations on-line and elaborating upon them, rendering the accessed and elaborated information available for input into the MTL memory system.We have argued that this content-sensitive pattern of PFC activation reflects the recruitment of distinct frontal processes that allocate attention to semantic, phonological, and visuo-spatial representations, guiding their input into declarative memory [Wagner, 1999; 2002].Consistent with this hypothesis, we have observed that these content-sensitive encoding patterns in PFC are accompanied by correlated patterns in posterior neocortical association areas that putatively represent the stimulus features being encoded [Kichhoff et al., 2000; see also, Dobbins & Wagner, in press].Our results revealed that transient disruption of left VLPFC function during verbal encoding impairs memory performance 20 min later, whereas disruption of right VLPFC enhanced later memory performance perhaps by inducing a functional shift to reliance on left-lateralized PFC control processes that are more effective for verbal encoding [Kahn et al., 2005]. We are actively pursuing open questions surrounding the role of PFC control processes in memory formation, including efforts to more precisely specify the impact of PFC processes in modulating posterior neocortical and MTL mechanisms.The contributions of cognitive control to episodic memory are not restricted to the building of memories, but also extend to episodic retrieval––that is, the ability to recollect contextual details surrounding a prior event or to detect stimulus novelty or familiarity. Our efforts to understand the interaction between cognitive control and declarative memory have included a focus on identifying and characterizing the multi-component nature of PFC contributions to retrieval with and without recollection.Relative to memory without recollection, source retrieval is thought to entail the recapitulation of neocortical representations present during the encoding of an event, and to differentially depend on strategic engagement of cognitive control. To test these hypotheses, we used fMRI to index neural activation during retrieval with and without source recollection. Our results revealed that (a) source recollection is associated with the recapitulation of representations in perceptual and conceptual processing regions that were engaged during initial encoding of events, (b) such recapitulation effects are observed not only for accurate remembrances, but also are present when we falsely recollect having encountered a novel stimulus, and (c) although PFC processes are differentially engaged during attempts to recollect, strategic engagement of these processes is gated by an initial assessment of whether the memory probe is familiar or novel [Kahn et al., 2004]. Results from a recently completed MEG study suggest that this familiarity-based gating of PFC function may emerge through an interaction with lateral parietal regions [Kahn et al., in prep; for a review of parietal cortex and episodic retrieval, see Wagner et al., 2005]. Collectively, these findings inform neural models of recollection, and address core debates surrounding cognitive theories of remembering.In a second line of investigation, we have begun to more precisely specify the nature of the PFC control mechanisms engaged during retrieval, focusing in on those that support “pre-retrieval processes” (e.g., representing and elaborating on retrieval cues in working memory) and those that operate “post-retrieval” (e.g., monitoring the products of retrieval as a basis for action) [Wagner, Desmond et al., 1998; Dobbins et al., 2002; Dobbins et al., 2003; Dobbins & Wagner, in press]. To this end, we first identified and characterized separable PFC structures that are recruited depending on whether a retrieval decision requires recollection of contextual details or an assessment of stimulus familiarity [Dobbins et al., 2003]. Our results revealed distinct left lateral PFC and parietal structures that distinguished attempted source recollection from judgments of relative stimulus familiarity, with these retrieval orientation effects being independent of retrieval outcome [for related strategic retrieval effects, see Wagner, Desmond et al., 1998]. Subsequently, we tested the nature of the left PFC processes recruited during source recollection [Dobbins et al., 2002; Dobbins & Wagner, in press]. Using conjunction analyses, we isolated multiple PFC retrieval responses, some that appear correlated with “pre-retrieval” mechanisms and some with “post-retrieval” mechanisms. In the former class, activation in distinct PFC regions was related to semantic analysis/cue specification (left anterior VLPFC), perceptual analysis/cue specification (right VLPFC), and cue maintenance (left posterior VLPFC). In the latter class, effects compatible with post-retrieval monitoring were observed in multiple structures (dorsolateral and frontopolar PFC).Though many questions remain, and an integrated model delineating how these putative mechanisms interact awaits specification, our investigations constitute initial progress towards specifying how PFC-mediated cognitive control processes support attempts to recollect the past. Our long-term goal is to develop an integrated model of the cascade of neural and cognitive events that give rise to episodic remembering.While episodic memory is modulated by PFC-mediated cognitive control mechanisms, it has long been known that episodic memory (and declarative memory, more broadly) most critically depends on the operations of the MTL memory system. The MTL is composed of multiple structures, including the hippocampal formation (dentate gyrus, fields of cornu Ammonis, and subiculum) and the surrounding entorhinal (ERc), perirhinal (PRc), and parahippocampal (PHc) cortices. Though extensive research has aimed to characterize the role of MTL in declarative memory, fundamental questions remain regarding the functional contributions of specific MTL substructures.Much of the debate centers on how the MTL encodes and retrieves conjunctive representations––which constitute item-context and item-item associations that can be pattern-completed during retrieval when given partial input––and the relation between these representations and those supporting item memory––knowledge about the individual items (elements) of an event and recognition that an item is novel or familiar.A core issue currently receiving considerable attention is whether conjunctive and item memory expression––as indexed by recollection and item familiarity, respectively––reflect quantitative or qualitative differences in the nature of the underlying memory representations, and, if the latter, whether these two forms of memory depend on separable components of the MTL memory system. From a dual-process perspective, the recollection of specific episodic details and the subjective sense of stimulus familiarity are qualitatively distinct (i.e., recollection and familiarity do not merely differ in degree of remembering, but rather differ in form). Neurally, one hypothesis is that the conjunctive representations supporting recollection depend on hippocampal auto-associative processes that encode the relation between event features and support later pattern completion, whereas item familiarity differentially depends on a match between the retrieval probe and MTL cortical representations of stored individual event elements.In an initial study [Davachi & Wagner, 2002], we reported that hippocampus is differentially engaged when encoding requires attention to the relations between items, with a subsequent memory analysis further revealing that the magnitude of hippocampal activation during relational encoding predicts later memory performance. By contrast, activation in MTL cortex (at or near PHc and ERc/PRc) is differentially greater when encoding stimuli as distinct items rather than when orienting to item-item relations. In a subsequent study of MTL encoding mechanisms [Davachi, Mitchell, & Wagner, 2003], we sorted fMRI encoding data according to subsequent item recognition and subsequent source recollection. Three critical findings were obtained. First, when sorting encoding data by subsequent item recognition (Recognized>Forgotten), independent of recollection, activation in anterior MTL cortex (at or near PRc) predicted later recognition, whereas activation in hippocampus failed to predict recognition. Second, when sorting the data according to subsequent source recollection (a measure of conjunctive memory), hippocampal activation predicted later recollection, whereas PRc activation did not. Third, this dissociation between PRc and hippocampus was accompanied by a pattern of activation in PHc that resembled that in hippocampus (rather than that in PRc), raising important questions as to the nature of PRc and PHc dissociations. These findings demonstrate that subregions within the MTL circuit support different forms of episodic encoding, and we are actively pursuing how best to characterize these distinct MTL mechanisms.At present, the neural mechanisms supporting perceived differences in memory strength at retrieval remain poorly specified. To begin to understand how memory strength is signaled, we used fMRI and MEG to index the neural correlates of graded memory strength in the human brain, focusing on MTL cortex [Gonsalves et al., 2005].The fMRI measures revealed decreased MTL cortical activation––observed along the anterior/posterior extent of the parahippocampal gyrus––that tracked parametric levels of perceived memory strength: Greater BOLD repetition suppression was associated with the perception of stronger item memory strength. These findings suggest that MTL cortex signals item memory strength via repetition suppression (or, conversely, signals stimulus novelty through increased activation).Building on these fMRI findings, our MEG data revealed that strength-dependent activation reductions can onset within 150-300 ms in MTL cortex, consistent with behavioral data revealing that evidence regarding item memory strength is rapidly available and consistent with electrophysiological data in animals showing rapid repetition suppression in PRc. Motivated by these fMRI and MEG observations, we are currently using high-resolution fMRI to test directed hypotheses regarding MTL retrieval processes supporting item memory strength, including examining (a) their dependence on study-test perceptual similarity, (b) the importance of stimulus-directed attention at encoding and retrieval for their emergence, and (c) whether distinct item memory effects are observed across MTL subregions. Consistent with this latter hypothesis, we recently obtained evidence pointing to a dissociation between conceptual and perceptual item memory effects along the anterior-posterior axis of parahippocampal gyrus [O’Kane et al., 2005].Extensive neuropsychological, electrophysiological, behavioral, and neuroimaging data indicate that memory is not a unitary system, but rather consists of multiple forms of learning and remembering that differ in their functional characteristics and neuroanatomic substrate.Memory research over that past two decades has placed an emphasis on identifying and dissociating memory systems, with less attention directed towards understanding when and how these different systems interact.Wagner et al., 2000]. Finally, studies of amnesic patients indicate that this repetition-induced decrease in left PFC activation reflects the operation of nondeclarative memory processes (i.e., priming).Taken together, these three observations suggest that priming may impair episodic encoding. We conducted an initial test of this hypothesis, observing a negative correlation between neural priming during re-encoding and the impact of this second encoding trial on later recognition memory [Wagner, Maril, & Schacter, 2000]. We are presently exploring the generality of this putative memory systems interaction, including a direct test of our hypothesis that priming hinders episodic encoding under some circumstances by reducing encoding variability.Our research into the cognitive neuroscience of memory aims to advance understanding of the complex cognitive and neural events that support memory, including interactions between cognitive control and memory and among multiple memory systems. Our initial investigations set the stage for the lab’s current efforts, which include (a) high-resolution functional imaging of human MTL [Preston et al., in prep], (b) computational specification of PFC cognitive control operations and their role in resolving proactive interference during task switching [Badre & Wagner, in prep-a] and in eliciting forgetting due to mnemonic filtering at retrieval [Kuhl et al., in prep], and (c) examination of putative interactions between PFC, MTL, and striatal systems during episodic and incremental learning [Shohamy et al., in prep]. We have also begun to extend our research to explore (a) neurocognitive aging, examining age-related deficits in mnemonic filtering of MTL retrieval processes [Badre & Wagner, in prep-b], and (b) functional changes in MTL substructures that accompany schizophrenia [Preston et al., 2005; Tamminga et al., in prep]. Collectively, we anticipate that these lines of research will further illuminate how the mind and brain give rise to the phenomenal cognitive abilities that we refer to as ‘memory’, as well as an understanding of how aging and disease-related processes impact these abilities.In order to facilitate planning, we ask that all registrations and abstracts arrive by July 15th. All relevant abstracts received by July 15th will be accepted. The main aim of the College's Green travel plan is actively to promote walking, cycling and the use of public transport for staff, students and visitors travelling to Birkbeck. This plan has been developed in response to Planning Policy Guidance note 13 (PPG13 (transport)) which states that…"The Government want to help raise awareness of the impacts of travel decisions and promote the widespread use of travel plans amongst businesses, schools, hospitals and other organisations."Review Transport Accessibility5. This new feature has been described by phrases such as "the non-separability of spatially separated systems", or more briefly as "quantum non-locality".  These terms are actually inadequate expressions of the radical implications of the notion of wholeness and reflect a strong desire to cling to a reductionist philosophy.  A radically new approach is needed, an approach that does not depend upon the Cartesian Order, but requires the introduction of new orders such as the implicate order and the generative order.  Mathematical descriptions of these new orders are under active development at present.It is now quite clear that if gravity is to be quantised successfully, a radical change in our understanding of spacetime will be needed.  We begin from a more fundamental level by taking the notion of process as our starting point.  Rather than beginning with a spacetime continuum, we introduce a structure process which, in some suitable limit, approximates to the continuum. We are exploring the possibility of describing this process by some form of non-commutative algebra, an idea that fits into the general ideas of the implicate order.  In such a structure, the non-locality of quantum theory can be understood as a specific feature of this more general a-local background and that locality, and indeed time, will emerge as a special feature of this deeper a-local structure.The London economy is diverse. 1.6 million people work in central London, with employment opportunities forecast to increase by 88,000 by 2007. Half of those employed have a qualification at NVQ level 4 or 5 (degree or above). The business and financial services dominate, but there are other growth areas such as the creative, health and leisure industries. The majority of the businesses in London are SMEs (over 80% of the members of the London Chamber of Commerce have fewer than 50 employees) and 19% of businesses are owned by individuals or families from Black or Asian ethnic groups. According to Focus Tec's Skills Action Plan for London (July 1999), less than half of all employers have any links with education or training providers.Labour Force Survey data illustrates that the adult population in London is already much more highly qualified in Higher Education (HE) terms than the country as a whole. The qualification density in Central London is 50% higher than the national average and the proportion of the population qualified to level 4 is increasing. As a result the first degree market in London is now static. However, the market for postgraduate taught courses is growing at 2.8% per annum and there remains a proportion of the population who wish to undertake HE but do not have the necessary skills, experience or educational background to enter a Bachelor degree course.Information Services Trust (HEIST) market survey funded through the Birkbeck Employer Advice and Guidance Link (EAGL) project (HEROBC) indicated that in London the high growth subjects for taught courses are health, computer science, engineering and technology, creative arts, architecture, and humanities. In addition to these courses Birkbeck has also developed Foundation Degree programmes to provide more part-time study opportunities in subjects where skills shortages exist in the London job market, specifically the biosciences, IT, media and management studies.College is to provide part-time courses of study to meet the changing educational, cultural and training needs of adults who are engaged in earning their livelihood and to enable adult students from diverse social and educational backgrounds to participate in our courses.Unlike other institutions offering part-time degrees, Birkbeck offers its programmes in the evenings and occasionally by day release: it concentrates on face-to-face rather than distance learning. This gives those, who for whatever reason, were unable to take up a degree at an earlier stage the opportunity to experience a full university education both academically and socially while continuing their employment or other day-time responsibilities.Hence the student population is composed almost totally of mature part-time students (99%) many of whom remain in employment while undertaking their course of study. An analysis of Birkbeck student data shows that their ages range from 18 to over 70 years with the majority falling within the 30-39 year age group.HEFCE produced performance indicators state that the number of mature part-time undergraduate entrants with no previous HE and from low participation neighbourhoods is significantly lower than the benchmark and so the College does not receive postcode premium funding. However, student records indicate that over 45% of Birkbeck first degree mature students have no previous HE even though they do not live in postcode areas identified by the 1991 census data as neighbourhoods of low participation.The ethnicity mix of students appears to vary widely between faculties with the Faculty of Social Sciences having a more diverse population than the other faculties. However, the College currently only collects ethnicity data in accordance with the HESA regulations and so a large section of the student population is characterised by colour i.e. "white" rather than ethnicity which makes a complete analysis of the student population impossible at this time.The diverse nature of the student population at Birkbeck impacts on the type and level of student support required. Mature part-time students trying to cope with the conflicting demands of work and financial and domestic responsibilities often require more support than full time school leavers.The College recognises the importance of providing a stimulating and supportive environment to encourage learning and therefore enable its students to successfully complete their studies. The College, both centrally and at faculty level together with the Student Union provide a range of support from financial help to study skills.Birkbeck has an established track record of providing financial support to enable students to enter and stay on course and achieve their potential. This support has long been part of the College's strategy for facilitating participation in higher education by financially disadvantaged groups, for example those in poorly paid employment, part-time or intermittent contract work, those with health or family difficulties.The student awards office has been expanded from 1FTE to the present staffing level of 3.2FTE in order to respond to the increasing number of students needing advice and financial help. Those using Birkbeck's financial support service expect and obtain a high level of sympathetic, knowledgeable, up-to-date face-to-face assistance which is integrated with the support offered by the Student Union. Awards officers review their performance in regular discussions and weekly staff training meetings, and have developed a working manual to ensure a consistent service.Birkbeck has established a Disability Office (2000) and the appointment of a Disability Co-ordinator and assistant to provide advice and guidance to prospective and current students who might otherwise not have the opportunity to take up or continue in higher education. This has enabled Birkbeck to take full advantage of government initiatives such as the extension of Disabled students allowance to part-time students. The Disability Officer also works closely with the Mental Health Support Officer who is part of the Widening Participation project to widen access to those with mental health needs.Union Presidents have liased closely with College academic and administrative staff resulting in an integrated system of student support and two-way communication of advice on matters of student welfare and student complaints. For further information please click here.Linda Melvern is one of Britain's leading investigative journalists and Honorary Professor in the Department of International Politics at the University of Wales, Aberystwyth. Professor Melvern was a consultant to the Military One prosecution team at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), and a part of her archive of documents on the planning and preparation of the genocide form a substantial part of the documentary evidence used by the prosecution in the trial.A new three-year research project aims to examine the cultural and artistic complexity of the caf as urban space, both in terms of turn-of-the-century Vienna and the fabric of twenty-first century cities. Caf culture is very much part of contemporary urban living and an understanding of its special place as a cultural nexus in Vienna will add much to our understanding not only of history, but also of ourselves.This multi-disciplinary project will investigate the social and artistic interactions that took place in and around the fin-de-siècle Viennese café, a key site of turn-of-twentieth century modernity. It functioned as both home and workplace, affording opportunities not only for leisure but also intellectual exchange. The researchers will explore the Viennese café as a threshold of space between public and private urban life, not only the architectural interior but also the boundaries between late nineteenth and early twentieth century ‘high’ and ‘low’ culture. The Viennese café as a vibrant and creative environment will be related to the café today as a key site for communication, community and the creation of urban culture.The project also aims to examine Viennese turn-of-the-century modernism in order to formulate alternative metaphors of modernity to those offered by the dominant discourses of art history, which have tended to focus on Paris. Since Baudelaire, the figure that has come to stand as modernity personified is the flâneur, who strolls around the city ‘botanizing on the asphalt’ (Walter Benjamin). The project proposes an alternative paradigm, that of the coffee house habitué who sits and awaits the arrival of the world at his table. This apparently more static metaphor of modernity is one that encourages an understanding of modern life as dissonant and psychologically fluid.The project will result in an international conference and an exhibition in 2008, accompanied by a series of musical and literary performances and followed by a major publication in 2009. The exhibition is not primarily centred on objects, but rather aims to present visual material within a multi-media environment in order to explore the complexities of the caf as an urban discursive space.Professor Christopher Frayling, Rector at the Royal College of Art states, "We are very excited at the Royal College of Art about this research project on the Viennese Café and its significance – which will bring together cultural history, the history of design and the work of the design studios at the College. For those of the current generation who thought the coffee house started life with Starbucks, this will come as quite an eye-opener."Johannes Wimmer, Director of the Austrian Cultural Forum, London, adds: “Although the first coffeehouses opened in London some 30 years earlier than in Vienna, their tradition appears to have lasted longer in the latter and, remarkably, almost became synonymous with a very special kind of Central European urban culture and way of life. The Austrian Cultural Forum London is delighted to be associated with The Viennese Café and Fin-de-siècle Culture research project, which will not only highlight an intense and hugely creative period in Vienna's cultural history, but also aim at taking a fresh look at urban modernity and its metaphors."Can we find the roots of culture in the roots of language? Click here for undergraduate and postgraduate programmes.Ji-Sung Park was seen by some as a controversial signing when he first arrived at Manchester United back in 2005, but new research carried out at Birkbeck reveals that South Korea’s leading player has helped Manchester United reinforce its position as Asia’s favourite European football club.The research, which has been undertaken by the Birkbeck Sport Business Centre (BSBC), shows that Manchester United enjoys overwhelming support in South Korea. Almost 75% of South Korean football fans selected Manchester United as their favourite European football team. The ‘Park Effect’ has had a significant impact on this result, with many fans stating that he is one of the main reasons they support the Red Devils. Dr Simon Chadwick, who led the research team and is also a Co-Director of the BSBC, states: “The signing of Ji-Sung Park has been good for Manchester United. He is not only a talented player, but he has also helped United strengthen its position in South Korea. At a time when many commentators are closely monitoring Manchester United’s financial performance, this research is good news for the club.”Park is not the only reason for South Korea’s interest in Manchester United. The strong heritage of the club, the excitement that is often associated with United games and a detailed knowledge of the team, were also identified as being an important factors influencing club support. Dr Chadwick stresses: “South Koreans seem keen to support their star players who perform at the top level in European football. PSV Eindhoven, from whom United signed Ji-Sung Park, were commonly identified as their second favourite European team. A club nevertheless still needs to play an exciting brand of football, and have a strong and clear heritage, if it is really to be popular in South Korea.”The research is also good news for English football in general; 66% of South Korean football fans said they regularly watch the Premier League on television (compared to 2% for the Bundesliga and 1.6% for Spanish La Liga football). Almost 45% of fans also said that they would be prepared to pay a subscription to watch English football on television, the internet or their mobile phones (compared to 3% for La Liga and Italy’s Serie A respectively). Dr Chadwick explains: “There is a long history of English football being broadcast across the world. Clearly, the Premier League continues to benefit from this but the sport broadcasting market is becoming increasingly competitive. The Premier League should not be complacent, other sports and other football leagues are set to challenge it.”The research was undertaken during the summer by Dr Chadwick, and a team of South Korean researchers currently working at Birkbeck. The team travelled to South Korea to distribute questionnaires and carry out interviews with fans of European football in their home country. Almost 400 South Koreans participated in the study.In an earlier study undertaken by the BSBC during 2005, research conducted in China also showed strong levels of support for Manchester United. Shorter than the more traditional undergraduate degree, it is designed specifically to equip students with the key skills required by today’s employers. Foundation degrees offer students a vocational degree combining technical expertise, academic knowledge and transferable skills, either as a stand alone qualification (equivalent to an NVQ4 or Higher National Diploma) or as a pathway to an honours degree. Graduates of the Foundation Degree in Pharmacy are offered the opportunity to continue their studies at honours degree level on associated pathways should they wish.Joanne Martin, the programme co-ordinator at Westminster Kingsway College, says: “What makes this course unique in the UK is that it is designed for pharmacy technicians in their increasingly expanding and important roles in today’s and tomorrow’s workforces.”She continues: “Two characteristics that pharmacy technicians share is their dedication to their roles as technicians and their professional attitudes. She is also exploring the politics of costume and make-up.“Verbatim theatre, such as Bloody Sunday at the Tricycle Theatre; site specific theatre, such as Shunt’s Tropicana at London Bridge station; and the Globe’s new artistic directorship are all changing the theatrical landscape of the city. The degree is of interest to those who work in the profession as performers, directors, designers and administrators, offering them the opportunity to understand the theories and histories behind what they do, as well as those who wish to move into another career, such as teaching, media work or further scholarship. It will also appeal to people in any industry who want a University of London qualification and are interested in the arts and theatre. All undergraduate teaching takes place in the evening, so students are able to work full-time while they study, gaining valuable work experience as they go and graduating without debt.What unspoken promises have you made to your employer and what unspoken promises have they made to you? Our written employment contracts only reveal some of what we do at work. The psychological contract is about the unwritten or implicit deals between employers and employees. When these deals are broken or violated it can lead to anger, disappointment, frustration and make employees feel less committed and motivated.A new book, Understanding Psychological Contracts, written by Dr Neil Conway and Professor Rob Briner from the School of Management and Organizational Psychology at Birkbeck, recently published in the US and UK by Oxford University Press, explores this fascinating subject. It is the first book to provide a comprehensive and critical overview of what is now the major way of understanding the employment relationship. The book examines issues such as what happens when these employment relationships go wrong between employer and employee, and considers the practicalities of using the psychological contract to manage people. "Written contracts often specify very little in terms of the important details about what we are prepared to do for our employer and what we want back in return. Our book considers these implicit or unwritten aspects of the employment relationship," says Professor Briner. "Employees may believe that if they work hard their organization will, in return, want to retain them and reward them fairly. A key idea that has emerged is that of psychological contract violation, when an employee believes that their organization has failed to deliver a promise to them. If an employee believes that his/her psychological contract has been breached, they will feel angry, let down, and are likely to feel less committed and motivated in their jobs."Starting with a history of the concept, from its emergence in the 1960s through to it finding wider acceptance in the 1990s, the authors trace the conflicting and changing definitions of the psychological contract. The book explores what employees really do expect from work; the dynamics of this relationship between an employee and their employer; whether the idea is of practical value in managing employees; and how our understanding of this important concept can be developed in the future. The authors add: "We go beyond the theory and research to consider areas not previously examined, for example, how psychological contracts unfold on a day-to-day basis and how the balance of these unspoken contracts can change subtly.""For example, an employee can feel let down about some issue at work and take a day off. Not being inclined to go to work can be due to a number of factors, such as wanting to get back at the organization for something it has done or not done for you, so that you don’t feel so committed to the organization, or you feel demoralized about your job. When an employee believes that the organization has failed to deliver its promises on a regular basis, he or she will question whether it makes sense to continue contributing to that organization or whether it might be better for them to move on to another."This book pulls together and synthesizes everything that is currently known about the psychological contract, as well as using new research to help illustrate key points.For further details, contact:Professor Rob Briner: 020 7631 6755Dr Neil Conway: 020 7631 6744For media enquiries, contact:Catherine Stevens, Media and Publicity OfficerTel: 020 7631 6569Email: c.stevens@bbk.ac.ukNOTES TO EDITORSSchool of Management and Organizational Psychology:The School of Management and Organizational Psychology is a highly successful and fast-growing section of Birkbeck. This work is coupled with wide-ranging outreach programmes to bring this material to audiences in schools, community and voluntary groups, museums, libraries and archives.The Big Lottery Fund brings together the work of two National Lottery distributors: the Community Fund, which provides funding for charities and the voluntary and community sectors, and the New Opportunities Fund for health, education and environment projects.Only female mosquitoes feed on blood, which they use as a source of protein for egg development. The amount of blood consumed in a single meal is equivalent to several times the body weight of an unfed mosquito, and therefore greatly restricts her manoeuvrability, making her more prone to predators.Work in the laboratory of Klaus Beyenbach (Cornell University) in the 1980s showed that feeding triggers the release of a hormone into the mosquito's circulatory system, which stimulates the excretion of excess salt and water. They named this hormone Mosquito Natriuretic Peptide (MNP), but were unable to characterise it further. However, I and my colleague Dave Schooley (Biochemistry Department, University of Nevada, Reno) have now identified this hormone in the malaria mosquito.The 'Ensembl' genome browser was used to search the genome of the malaria mosquito for sequences resembling those of previously identified fruit fly hormones. Two likely candidates for MNP were found, one made up of 31 amino acids (DH31), and the other comprising 44 amino acids (DH44). Both were synthesised in Dave Schooley's laboratory and then sent to me at Birkbeck's School of Biological and Chemical Sciences in order for me to evaluate their biological activity.The two peptides thought to stimulate excretion were tested for their effect on urine secretion using isolated Malpighian tubules, which are the mosquito's equivalent of our kidneys. While one peptide looked promising by increasing urine production, there was no specific stimulation of sodium excretion.By contrast, and much to our delight, the hormone of 31 amino acids – the DH31 – not only dramatically increased fluid secretion, but also specifically stimulated sodium excretion. Indeed, the activities of this hormone precisely replicate those of MNP discovered in the 1980s.The number of deaths resulting from malaria each year is estimated to be two million, of which almost half are children. With resistance to drugs on the rise, controlling the mosquito population remains an important weapon in the fight against malaria.Unfortunately, mosquitoes are resistant to many of the insecticides now in use, which mainly target the nervous system. There is therefore an urgent need to identify new and specific targets for mosquitocides, and the dramatic effects of this newly discovered hormone on salt and water excretion suggest that this find could be an important lead.Sir Gareth is Chair of the Higher Education Funding Council for England’s Research Committee, which led the UK-wide review of the Government’s Research Assessment Exercise. The Certificate and Diploma programme in Understanding London explore the nature of contemporary London, the social problems of today and the opportunities for the future. We will speak to you first before we approach your contact.Matthew Innes has published widely on the history of Europe in the late antique and early medieval periods, that is from the fifth to the eleventh centuries CE. Geographically, his research has focused on north-western Europe, especially the Frankish kingdoms in modern France, Germany and the Low Countries, but is also encompasses the western Mediterranean, Britain, Scandinavia and east-central Europe. Published work has concentrated on two major issues. A series of articles and chapters have explored the ‘uses of the past’, that is the process whereby understandings of the past were reshaped so as to explain or interpret the present. Another strand of work has studied on the social relationships between aristocratic and ecclesiastical elites, royal courts and peasant communities, which determined cultural, economic and political dynamics; the resulting reinterpretation of the processes of ‘state-formation’ in post-Roman Europe has been a focus of international debate.Matthew’s contribution to the field was recognized by the award of a Philip Leverhulme Prize in 2004 ( http://www.leverhulme.ac.uk/news/past_prizes/2004 ) and his case-study of society and politics in the Rhine valley under Carolingian rule was awarded the Royal Historical Society’s Gladstone History Book Prize in 2000. His current research investigates the structures of early medieval society as revealed by documentary evidence, and in particular the relationships between property ownership, legal freedom and public power. A series of studies on ‘practices of property’, embracing not only the rich evidence from the Carolingian Empire which was the mainstay of his earlier work, but also the surviving material from the barbarian successor states which emerged in the immediately post-Roman west, have been facilitated by the support of the Leverhulme Trust.Matthew would be interested in supervising proposals on any aspect of late antique or early medieval western European history. Matthew has successful experience of gaining postdoctoral studentships from the Arts and Humanities Research Council, and can also offer advice on the various sources of support available from Birkbeck’s School of History.The text is centrally important in its context within Old Norse/Icelandic historiography, an area which is becoming increasingly prominent in the field (besides Morkinskinna, a range of earlier synoptic texts in Norse or Latin have recently appeared in English, and all these historical texts attracted considerable interest at the International Saga Conference in Norway in 1997); and merits further study in terms of its relationship with Heimskringla, which was probably written independently (in Iceland) but making use of common sources. Fagrskinna also has implications for the discussion of the development of vernacular narrative writing in the Sagas of Icelanders (Family Sagas), particularly in terms of its extensive use of skaldic verse sources.A considerable number of skaldic stanzas dating from considerably before the prose narrative itself are preserved only in Fagrskinna, and closer study of this text will provide information about their context. The difficulty of understanding, let alone translating satisfactorily, this intricate verse form probably helps to explain why the text has not been translated before, and represents a considerable challenge for the translator. The proposed translation will aim to emphasize the centrality of this verse as a source for, and an instrument in the construction of, medieval Norse narrative texts, both historical works and those that by modern definitions would be considered literary.SIGNIFICANCE: This essential text, only relatively recently available in a modern readable edition, has been largely ignored by historians and literary scholars, and overshadowed by the more readily accessible Heimskringla. Its appearance in English is important particularly because of its relevance to historical as well as literary study. Natural History Museum, see Bristow in press, Bristow and Hill in press, and Whybrow et al. in press.My research concerns how people reason and construct arguments in discourse. From a logical point of view, people seem to make many errors and biases in their deductive reasoning. However, from a probabilistic point of view, these “errors” are the rational result of people being more sensitive to the strength of an argument defined using Bayesian probability theory rather than to deductive validity. This approach can also be generalised to account for the differential strength of the informal argument fallacies that have accrued in logic text books since Aristotle. This research involves experimental work and modelling the resulting inferential behaviour. I am also interested in how the emotions, both experienced and anticipated, affect people’s reasoning and decision making.Informing the College of any changes to information that they have provided, e.g. changes of address, either at the time of appointment or subsequently. For example, you cannot claim for any medicines.Non-medical helper"s allowance: this is an annual allowance, which pays for support by personal assistants (e.g. note-takers, interpreters, readers or dyslexia tutorial support, etc.) required so that you can benefit fully from your course. The Master shall be assisted by the Registrar as Secretary of the Academic Board.  Any candidate in an election may nominate a scrutineer.Under Statute 3(c) (i) and (ii), three Representative Governors are elected by the Academic Board from amongst the Professors and Readers and three are elected by and from amongst the full-time members of the Academic Staff other than Professors or Readers.B.1.1.3	Notification shall be by a notice sent by the Returning Officer to each member of the Academic Board designated "Election of a Representative Governor to serve from (date) upon the retirement of (name) of (School)/ to fill the casual vacancy arising from (cause, name and School) until (date)", calling for nominations to fill the vacancy to be submitted to him/her by a date twenty-one days later than the date of the notice.  The notice shall state the name and Schools of the two continuing Governors and shall draw attention to any formal resolutions of the Academic Board on the desirability of maintaining a balance of subject representation.B.1.3	If only one nomination is received, the Returning Officer shall declare the result forthwith by notice on the College Notice Board and shall report it to the next meeting of the Academic Board.  If the vacancy is contested, he/she shall forthwith send to each candidate a list of candidates with the names of their proposers and seconders and shall notify them of his/her intention to conduct an election.  Having taken note of any withdrawals, he/she/ shall as soon as possible, conduct the election by postal ballot on the system of the single transferable vote.  The poll shall remain open for seven days.  In the event of a tie, the Returning Officer shall determine the election by the toss of a coin.  He/she shall declare the result forthwith by notice on the College Notice Board and shall report it to the next meeting of the Academic Board.B.1.4	If by the due date the Returning Officer has received no response to his/her call for nominations made under paragraph B.1.1 above, he/she shall cause to be included in the agenda paper of the next meeting of the Academic Board a statement that he/she will call for oral nominations to be made at the meeting and the vacancy shall be filled by resolution or by ballot at that meeting.Under Statute 4(b), the Representative Governors elected by the full-time members of the Academic Staff other than Professors and Readers shall be elected from members of the electing body under such rules of procedure as the Governors in consultation with the Academic Board shall direct.B.2.2.3	Notification shall be by a notice sent by the Returning Officer to each full-time member of the Academic Staff other than Professors and Readers, designated "Election of a Representative Governor to serve from (date) upon the retirement of (name) of (School)/ to fill the casual vacancy arising from (cause, name and School) until (date)", calling for nominations to fill the vacancy to be submitted to him/her by a date twenty-one days later than the date of the notice.  The notice shall state the name and Schools of the two continuing Governors and shall draw attention to any formal resolutions of the Academic Board on the desirability of maintaining a balance of subject representation.  The notice shall also include a statement of the convention adopted by the Board whereby Faculty Deans are requested not to accept nomination for election as a Representative Governor elected by the full-time members of the Academic Staff and a reminder that the election of such a Representative Governor is in effect also the election of a representative on the Academic Board Executive Committee.B.2.4	If only one nomination is received, the Returning Officer shall declare the result forthwith by notice on the College Notice Board and shall report it to the next meeting of the Academic Board.  If the vacancy is contested, he/she shall forthwith send to each candidate a list of candidates with the names of their proposers and seconders and shall notify them of his/her intention to conduct an election.  Having taken note of any withdrawals, he/she shall as soon as possible conduct the election by postal ballot on the system of the single transferable vote.  The poll shall remain open for seven days.  In the event of a tie, the Returning Officer shall determine the election by the toss of a coin.  He/she shall declare the result forthwith by notice on the College Notice Board and shall report it to the next meeting of the Academic Board.B.2.5	If by the due date the Returning Officer has received no response to his/her call for nominations made under paragraph B.2.2 above, he/she shall issue a second call for nominations.  If he/she receives no response to his/her second call, he/she shall declare the vacancy, which may be filled by any eligible person properly nominated and seconded unopposed.  The result shall be reported to the next meeting of the Academic Board.  The end of the term of office of the person so elected shall be that specified in the first call for nominations.By resolution of the Academic Board with the concurrence of the Governors, in accordance with Statute 32(e), the Academic Staff other than Professors and Readers (i.e. the Senior Lecturers and Lecturers) in each School, not being Faculty Deans, annually appoint to representative membership of the Academic Board one person from among their own number if their number, disregarding the duly elected Head of School be seven or fewer; if their number, disregarding the duly elected Head of School, be eight or more, they may appoint one additional representative member of the Academic Board; if their number, disregarding the duly elected Head of School, be fifteen or more, they may appoint two additional representative members of the Academic Board.  Each person so elected shall be the holder of a post-probationary appointment in the College unless there is no other lecturer or senior lecturer in the School who is not an ex-officio member of the Academic Board.  The Library Staff of academic status, other than the Librarian and Deputy Librarian, annually appoint to representative membership of the Academic Board a person or persons from among their own number in the same terms as if they were the members of a School.  The Faculty of Continuing Education academic-related staff with quasi-academic roles annually appoint to representative membership of the Academic Board one person from among their own number.C.1.1.1  The Head of each School shall ensure that arrangements are made for the representative(s) to be duly elected by those Senior Lecturers and Lecturers of the School who are eligible under these provisions and that the names of duly elected representatives are reported to the Returning Officer by the last day of June.C.1.1.2  If an uncontested nomination is made by the Senior Lecturers and Lecturers of a School the Head of the School shall report the nomination to the Returning Officer as the duly appointed representative.C.1.1.3  If contested nominations are made by the Senior Lecturers and Lecturers of a School the Head shall make arrangements for the conduct of an election on the system of the single transferable vote and shall report the result.C.1.1.4  If by the due date the Returning Officer has received no response to his/her call for nominations made under paragraph C.1.1 above, he/she shall declare that there is no representative of the School concerned elected to membership of the Academic Board under these provisions for the session concerned.C.1.2.  The Librarian shall proceed in a manner analogous to the procedure prescribed for Heads of Schools in paragraphs C.1.1.1 to C.1.1.3 in respect of the election of representative(s) of Library staff of academic status, other than the Librarian and Deputy Librarian.C.1.3	Each year no later than the end of the first week of the Summer Term the Returning Officer shall send to the Dean of the Faculty of Continuing Education a notice designated "Election of a representative of Faculty of Continuing Education academic-related staff with quasi-academic roles to membership of the Academic Board", calling for the name of the duly elected representative to be reported to him/her by the last day of June.  The Dean shall proceed in a manner analagous to the procedure prescribed for Heads of Schools in paragraphs C.1.1.1 to C.1.1.3 in respect of the election of the representative of Faculty of Continuing Education Academic-related staff with quasi-academic roles.By resolution of the Governors, it is provided that the appointment of the Dean be for five years or to the date of his/her final retirement, whichever is the shorter period; a Dean who has served for a period of office but who has not reached the date of his/her final retirement is eligible for re-election.  In cases where the term of office comes to an end on a date other than 30 September, the period of appointment of the successor will be to 30 September of the academic session in which five years of office are completed.D.2.1.1	In the case of the forthcoming expiration of the term of office of the Dean, notification shall be given not later than the eighth week of the Spring term preceding the date of the expiration.  If the office of Dean falls vacant for any other reason, notification shall be given at the earliest practicable date following receipt of the notice of a vacancy from the Secretary of the College.D.2.1.2  Notification shall be by a notice sent by the Returning officer to each member of the Academic Board designated "Election for the Nomination to the office of Dean to succeed Professor ....", calling for nominations to fill the vacancy to be submitted to him/her by a date twenty-one days later than the date of the notice.D.2.3	If only one nomination is received, the Returning Officer shall report the result to the next meeting of the Academic Board.  If the vacancy is contested, he/she shall forthwith send to each candidate a list of candidates with the names of their proposers and seconders and shall notify them of his/her intention to conduct an election.  Having taken note of any withdrawals, he/she shall as soon as possible conduct the election by postal ballot on the system of the single transferable vote.  The poll shall remain open for seven days.  In the event of a tie, the Master, as Chairman of the Board, shall exercise a casting vote.  The result shall be reported to the next meeting of the Academic Board.D.2.4	If a nomination by the Board has been duly made and if the nomination has the approval of the Master, it shall be forwarded to the Governors at their next meeting.  If the Board has failed to make a nomination, or if the nomination by the Board has not the approval of the Master, there shall be a re-notification of the election in accordance with the procedures set out in paragraphs 2.1 to 2.3 above, the dates to be suitably amended by the Returning Officer.By resolution of the Governors, it is provided that the appointment of the Vice-Master be for five years with the possibility of re-appointment for a further period of up to three years.  In cases where the term of office comes to an end on a date other than 31 July, the initial period of appointment of the successor will be to 31 July of the academic financial year in which five years of office are completed.In the Summer term of the Vice-Master's fourth year of office, there shall be consultation between the Master and the Vice-Master on the extension of the term of office; if they agree that it should be extended the Academic Board shall be notified at its June meeting and a recommendation for extension shall be brought to the June/July meeting of Governors; if either or both do not wish the appointment to be extended or if Governors do not approve the recommendation, the procedure for nomination set out in 2 shall be set in motion in the Autumn term following.About the QAA: "Our mission is to safeguard the public interest in sound standards of higher education qualifications and to encourage continuous improvement in the management of the quality of higher education. We do this by working with higher education institutions to define academic standards and quality, and we carry out and publish reviews against these standards.We were established in 1997 and are an independent body funded by subscriptions from UK universities and colleges of higher education, and through contracts with the main UK higher education funding bodies. An overview of our work can be found at: QAA: an introduction (external site)"To meet the needs of Birkbeck's students and staff in pursuit of the College's aim to provide quality, research-led higher education to a wide range of mainly part time, mature students over a broad range of subjects.To adopt an approach of integrating as far as possible measures and methods into routine procedures to reinforce both the philosophy and the practice of quality assurance and enhancement as an integral part of normal business.To provide an accessible and effective infrastructure for dealing with quality assurance at the institutional level and for disseminating good practice. This includes ensuring that staff are familiar with the quality assurance procedures and mechanisms in place.The College's codes of practice describe the responsibilities of individual members of staff (including Programme Directors and Heads of Schools), teams, groups, Schools, committees and others. They are intended to provide a comprehensive 'reference manual' that will be of use to all staff by providing permanently available and regularly updated guidance on key aspects of the assurance and enhancement of Birkbeck's quality and standards.Programme specifications have been developed at Birkbeck to meet the requirements of the QAA and HEFCE to provide public information, in a short and concise format, which may be used by all potential stakeholders including current and prospective students, employers, professional and statutory bodies, institutions and teaching teams, academic reviewers and external examiners.The College's template for programme proposals takes the form of a combined programme proposal/programme specification form. The form therefore attempts to bring together, into a coherent whole, the planning work with regard to academic content, resource allocation, academic regulations and marketing prior to implementation of a new programme whilst also covering the requirements of a programme specification.Programme specifications play a key role in internal and external reviews including  Institutional Audit which examines "the accuracy, completeness and reliability of the information, including programme specifications, that an institution publishes about the quality of its programmes and the standards of its awards" (QAA, March 2002).In 2000/01 the Quality Assurance Committee decided to design and implement a College wide system of gathering student feedback. This decision was taken in order to achieve some degree of College-wide consistency in the design of the questionnaires that students are asked to complete; and to reflect best practice in eliciting information about our students' learning experience and how it might be enhanced and improved.The QAC recommends that Schools should provide students with four types of opportunity to comment formally on their learning experience and to offer advice about how teaching provision might be enhanced. The questionnaires may be contextualised to meet the specific requirements of each School. Those Schools that already have questionnaires in place may utilise these providing they elicit the required information set out in the questionnaires below.The annual programme reports, which must be completed for all taught degrees, include a section summarising action taken in response to student feedback e.g. student-staff exchange committee meetings, student feedback questionnaires and email communication.Internal reviews provide a means by which Schools can, in collaboration with members of the wider College community, review and enhance the quality of their academic provision. The process also enables the College to assess its policies for enhancing the student experience.Internal reviews of taught and research programmes (full-time, part-time and distance learning) are carried out at least once every four years. Wherever possible an internal review is scheduled as preparation for scrutiny by an external body such as a professional body accreditation visit or a QAA discipline audit trail.The process of annual programme monitoring reflects that of internal review and QAA guidelines and is intended to evaluate "student achievement of the appropriate academic standards, and of the learning opportunities offered to students to support their achievements" (Handbook for institutional audit: England 2002).Birkbeck requires annual programme reports to be completed on all taught degree programmes. The report should provide evidence on the basis of which to undertake a review of the programme, to assess whether its objectives are being realised and whether current practice can be improved and enhanced. The report should be written in the light of the Framework for Higher Education Qualifications (FHEQ); relevant sections of the QAA's Code of Practice and benchmark statements taking particular note of the features of specialised programmes, such as Foundation degrees and those involved with collaborative, flexible and distributed learning.The report should include developments that have taken place since the previous year's report and those which are currently in progress detailing how these have enhanced practice. The report should therefore show evidence of continuing improvement and development of the programme.Each report should be copied to the relevant Faculty Dean and a draft should be discussed at a relevant School committee (e.g. School meeting, School Teaching Committee) prior to submission to the Academic Quality Assurance Office by the published deadline.This page is designed to highlight areas of good practice within the College that have emerged through annual reports, programme specifications and other methods of quality assurance that are operated throughout the College. One or two academic members of staff usually attend and the School provides sundry expenses for light refreshments. The QAC recommends this as a good method of encouraging student work and helping to nurture a sense of community amongst research students. Either Chemistry or Biology must be included in your subjects chosen. The most common subject combinations are: Biology and Chemistry; and Chemistry and Mathematics. Other combinations are possible, for example to prepare for degrees in radiography, a combination of Biology and Physics is most appropriate.Parts I and II are assessed by coursework and tests only (with some assignments completed in class, for example laboratory experiments, and some at home); Part III includes both coursework and a final examination (taken in late May/early June).The 30 weeks of study for this subject, which is divided into three sequential 10-week modules (Parts I, II and III), will give you a lively and interesting introduction to the major themes in biology, including: the chemical and cellular basis of life; diversity, structure and function of bacteria, plants and animals; plant and animal physiology; genetics and evolution ecology. You will also develop essential skills such as observation, microscope and drawing techniques, and data handling.You need a good level of numeracy and English language skills for all the subject options. How do historians do research and communicate it? As social beings, can historians be objective? Should morality play any role in historical judgements? Is the present progress from the past? The module fee includes attendance at the Making History study day on Saturday, 14 October 2006.This module explores the writing of history (historiography) from the earliest historians through to postmodernism. Numerous new studies of patient experiences are currently underway. Responding to a wider trend to write history ‘from below’, scholars initially focused upon the role of the sick individual within the ‘medical marketplace’, in an effort to understand patients’ experiences of health and sickness.Only within the last few years has this new approach begun to be applied to the history of the hospital so as to incorporate new types of written and visual evidence and explore a much wider range of patient experiences than that embraced by earlier studies. Without the hard work of all of them, it would not have been possible for our association to make the progress we have on negotiating for the national pay framework, representing individual members, and conducting our recent pay campaign. It has been another hard year, as we have had to continue with the framework negotiations while taking part in the national pay campaign, and while our national association has been going through its merger with NATFHE. Despite all this, we have continued to represent our members locally and have added many new members through the pay campaign.Implementation of the 2004 national Framework Agreement has been, along with the national pay campaign, the most important issue for the local association over the past year. From the start it has been very difficult to keep members informed because of the tentative and confidential nature of this process. The UCU team comprises Nick Keep, Trevor Fenner, Kate Purcell and myself. During the past year, we have continued to take part in regular meetings of the Framework Negotiating Group (FNG), first on our own and then together with our colleagues in UNISION and AMICUS. The negotiations have been long and slow, with at least one meeting per month and more in recent months.Early in the year we reached a tentative agreement with management to a pay framework for academic and academic related staff based on the UCU’s alternative model but going beyond it if resources permit. Having reached that agreement, we began single table negotiations with the other unions UNISON and MSF-AMICUS on implementation of Job Evaluation. Two UCU members, Oya Biringen-Akman and Kate Mackenzie-Davey, were trained and then took part in job evaluation panels, a process which continued over several months. We have reached a stage where we are discussing very fine points of detail which could have a major impact on some of our members. We have been working for a clear, transparent, and fair process throughout, and are striving to represent the interests of all members to the best of our ability.March through 6 June, involving the boycott of assessment and appraisal, a refusal to cover for absent colleagues, and other measures, appears to have been well observed, but this is difficult to judge. The action was much stronger in some departments and schools than others. But most members do appear to have taken part in at least some of the actions, which we can all be proud of. Many of us were disappointed by the sudden suspension of the action on 6 June, and Birkbeck UCU is not making a recommendation either for or against the proposed settlement in the present ballot. I would like to thank all members for your participation in our industrial action, and also for your efforts in completing marking on time for most exam boards, showing once again our genuine concern for our students.Most of the real work with management over the past year has been in the framework negotiations, covered above. We have continued our usual termly meetings of the Academic Joint Committee (AJC), and have had regular informal meetings with Management on other matters. Nick Keep and I met the Master several times in the course of our pay dispute, which proved important in maintaining positive relations with management and in preventing any attempts to bring in strike-breakers or take reprisals against individual members for taking part in the action. We have had some positive settlements in personal cases over the past year, particularly for members working on the National Evaluation of Sure Start who were threatened with redundancy. The College Secretary, who took up office in September, has played a helpful role in these settlements and in other matters.Membership has gone up in the course of the national pay campaign, and some meetings have been well attended. There has been a positive response to the new Birkbeck Briefing, and good email contact with members, particularly during the pay dispute. However, the association continues to depend on a small number of committed activists, and there are not many new faces appearing each year. We need to hold another a membership recruitment drive, particularly among fixed term, research, and hourly paid staff, and find new ways to energise the membership as a whole. I’d like to thank Nick, Diane, Trevor, and Kate, and all committee members for your hard work, as well as our wise and efficient local official, Rob Jones.
